chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
title: 'Jazzing the classics' and vocal folk-song versions
summary: Kirby's instrumental classics followed 'Loch Lomond'; the folk-song swing treatment was simple but caught on.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Listening to classical music, then and now

blocks.x: Yes. Oh incidentally, we used the term I noticed in looking back over the early tapes, jazzing the classics okay, and that's kind of a very general term we used because it seems to me there are at least three things going on beyond that time, only one of which you were doing if I'm not mistaken. One would be making swing or jazz renditions of light classical music which I guess "Song of India" which Tommy Dorsey did, which was the first example, and many of the things that the Kirby Band did from "Chopin" and so on.
Yeah, Kirby actually got into those things after "Loch Lomond" because it became pretty

much of a fad by that time. I'm not sure that I might have been the first one to swing some of the traditional songs.
But that's the second kind of activity though, from this as to making instrumental performances.
Yes.
I think they used the word "swing- phonic" for that, didn't they?
Yes. Up until that time I suppose most of those renditions were just instrumental, orchestra arrangements. But actually until you sing one of them it's a different questions.
Yes.

"Loch Lomond" was such a simple melody and such a simple lyric, maybe nobody had thought about it before. Of course, then there was the controversy that arose that Ella Logan had sung "Loch Lomond" at the time I had. And that sort of, you know, made it more or less a matter of opinion. You see Ella Logan was definitely Scotch and she had a Scotch accent. I don't suppose anybody paid much attention to it. My
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
version of it was a little bit more bluesey I would say, and then the arrangement itself was different. And it was one of those things that caught on.

Anyway that's a different kind stringing the classics than the first thing I described, and this is making vocal renditions of Folk Songs, or at least not the kind of Alan Lomax folk songs in the field, but published folk songs that people had gone out and compiled and written down.
The folk songs you know were considered, the renditions of the folk songs were pretty authentic as they were intended to be.
Yeah.

But with a string arrangement behind it it made it a little different. And of course that was the height of the swing era and I think too that getting away from just the every day pop made a difference too. 'Lock Lomond' never did become a pop tune. It was always just that swing arrangement of 'Lock Lomond' The other pop tunes became dance arrangements which people danced to, maybe or maybe not, whether they put any lyrics to it or not they just put dance arrangements to

Anyway, talking about pop songs, there is a third thing again which is an expression of a similar kind of thing and that's the conversion of classical music melodies into pop songs by the addition of a pop lyric.
Yes.
Frank Sinatra had a song, 'Moon Dreams'?
Yes, you know way back in the early days Al Jolson did 'Avalon' years ago. And this was the theme of 'Avalon' was taken from a classical tune.
Yes.

So when you figure there's only a handful of notes to choose from that's why they have copyright laws so you don't just come right out and steal a melody but all you have to do is just change the rhythm of one note and you got a new song.
I don't recall on your records that you ever did, so good. Did you ever sing any of those third kinds of songs? You know, pop songs that were created out of classical?

No, most of the things that I did . . .
You stayed pretty much within the folk songs?
Yeah, and actually I just sang the melody. It was the band that was doing the swinging.
Anyway it brough you intense success.
It sure did.
